Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
This is a fair and well-organised synthesis. Its overall conclusion is the right one:

- per-hour gains are real but much smaller than the headline pilot figure;
- output per worker is roughly maintained in discretionary work but falls in coverage-bound work;
- neither "sector-general" nor "entirely an artifact" holds.

Its account of each source is mostly accurate. The problems are of three kinds. Some claims are stated more firmly than the sources allow, especially the meetings mechanism and the size of the decline. One arithmetic statement is inconsistent. And several caveats raised against the later sources have dropped out. Most important first:

## 1. The five sources are not five independent pieces of evidence

The briefing's framing ("read as a whole, the five sources") and its convergence argument suggest independent confirmation, but the sources overlap heavily:

- Sources 3 and 5 (Halden part) reuse source 1's data.
- Source 5 extends source 2.
- Source 4 includes sources 1 and 2.

The controlled evidence on discretionary work rests largely on one trial: Varden, with 7 treated and 7 control offices in one public employer. Source 4 adds only about four other controlled discretionary studies.

The briefing also says source 4's work-type moderator "generalises source 2." But Varden is itself among source 4's 23 studies, so the meta-analysis partly re-counts it. The same applies to the "convergence" on 8–10%: as I noted on source 4, the controlled, actual-hours and record-based subgroups are largely the same studies. The briefing should say plainly that the best evidence is one well-designed trial plus a thin controlled literature, and set its confidence accordingly.

## 2. The meetings mechanism is stated as established fact

§3.4 says about half the gain "comes from removing recurring meetings," and the Bottom line puts "about half of it through fewer meetings" into the headline policy statement. That goes beyond what source 5 can support:

- **The meeting cuts were not randomised.** The mediation result depends on the assumption that nothing else drove both meeting cuts and productivity, which source 5 itself acknowledges.
- **It is not an independent test.** The hypothesis came from the same seven offices in their first nine months. Registration makes it a pre-specified test, not a replication.
- **The interval is wide and possibly too narrow.** 47% has a CI of 28–66%. With 14 clusters, even that may understate the uncertainty.
- **It is unclear what the hours measure records.** Source 5 doesn't say whether system logs include meeting time, which affects how the meetings pathway should be read.
- **It is one setting.** The Bottom line generalises a result from one county's case-processing offices to discretionary work in general.

§3.4 could say instead: "In the one setting where it was tested, a pre-specified mediation analysis attributed roughly half the per-hour gain to fewer recurring meetings." The meetings figure should come out of the Bottom line, or be qualified there.

## 3. The size of the decline is overstated, and the control-office issue is missing

§1 says the Varden gain "declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)." That repeats the mixed-measure comparison in source 5's own Summary: the 12.5% is from timesheets, the 8.5% from logs. The like-for-like figures are 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets.

Two further caveats are missing:

- **The decline isn't statistically established.** The two intervals overlap substantially, and no test of the difference was reported.
- **Two control offices cut their meetings at month 15**, raising control productivity and so shrinking the measured treatment effect at 24 months. Part of the apparent decline may be the controls improving.

The second point appears in §4 only as weak evidence that reorganisation alone might work. The briefing doesn't mention that the same event also biases the main 24-month estimate.

§3.1's "some decline from the first year to the second" and §4's "the per-hour gain declined" should both be softened to something like "a decline is suggested but not established."

## 4. The per-worker arithmetic in §3.2 doesn't hold across the stated range

§3.2 says actual hours fall by 11–14% and the per-hour gain is 8–10%, giving per-worker output "around 2 to 4% lower." Output per worker equals (1 + per-hour gain) × (1 − hours cut):

| | Hours cut 11% | Hours cut 14% |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain 8% | −3.9% | −7.1% |
| Per-hour gain 10% | −2.1% | −5.4% |

The 2–4% figure is consistent only with an 11% cut, which is Varden's log measure. At 14%, losses are 5–7%. The cited per-worker estimates are themselves fine: Varden −3.4% and source 4's controlled discretionary −2.7%. The two ranges just don't reconcile with them.

Also, the intervals around those estimates reach −8.0% and −6.5%. "Close to true" for "same output in four days" should be paired with the fact that losses of 6–8% can't be ruled out.

## 5. Table 1 doesn't show what the text says it shows

The table is titled "ordered by strength of design," and the text says "estimates fall as designs strengthen." There are three problems:

- **It isn't strictly ordered.** The all-studies meta-analytic estimate (+13.4%) mixes designs, yet sits below two uncontrolled subsets.
- **The pattern isn't monotone.** The nine-month randomised estimate (+12.5%) is higher than both uncontrolled actual-hours estimates (+10.8%, +11.8%). The pattern the text describes holds broadly, but the table shows it less cleanly than claimed.
- **Rows differ in more than design.** They mix work types (sources 1 and 3 span six sectors; the last row is coverage-bound) and time points. "Stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work" draws on rows that are not all discretionary.

Splitting the table by work type, or adding columns for work type and follow-up length, would make the comparison honest. Source 4's controlled (+8.2%), actual-hours (+7.9%) and record-based (+9.7%) subgroups are cited in the text and could be added.

## 6. The verdicts on sources 3 and 4 are slightly too clean

- **Source 3's novelty claim** is said not to "survive later evidence." Its *strong* form ("entirely an artifact") does not survive. But source 5 found a decline suggestive of some fading, so source 3's concern was partly borne out. Saying so would be fairer and more informative.
- **Source 3's corrections** "stand," but with qualifications noted in my review of it. Its 10.8% does not correct for attrition, despite its abstract. Its hours breakdown didn't add up. Its record-based output included billable hours, which falls mechanically when hours are cut.
- **The attrition finding** (seven of nine withdrawals after the schedule started) hasn't been confirmed or answered by the Halden authors. Source 5 had a Halden co-author and didn't address it. The briefing should note that it remains unanswered rather than treat it as settled.
- **Source 4's "no decay" claim** is called "wrong." Source 5 showed it was *unsupported*: the four studies couldn't speak to decay. Whether decay occurs remains open, as §4 itself says.

## 7. Wellbeing claims carry over known problems

§3.5 calls the falls in sickness and resignations "real benefits," found in "every source that measured them." Three caveats:

- **The 36% upper bound is Halden's.** That figure is uncontrolled, not adjusted for seasonality, and may fall partly mechanically: shorter schedules leave fewer days on which to be absent.
- **No source resolved the mechanical issue.** The controlled estimates (Varden −27 to −29%) are more credible, but they too count sick days rather than hours lost against hours scheduled.
- **Resignations.** Halden's fall coincided with a cooling labour market. Varden's estimate is imprecise.

The direction is consistent. "Likely real, with the size uncertain" is the accurate level of confidence.

## 8. Missing from §4 (what the body leaves open)

- **Cost.** No source estimates cost per unit of output in discretionary work, even though full pay plus overtime with slightly lower output per worker implies higher unit costs. The only cost figure is the county's estimate for counter work (+12% staff, +9% cost per contact), which §3.3 presents as a general finding. It should be marked as one employer's estimate.
- **Statistical precision.** The randomised estimates come from 10–14 clusters. Standard cluster-robust errors are likely too narrow at that size, and no source reports corrected inference.
- **Size of the cut.** The briefing addresses a 20% cut. Source 4 includes cuts of 10% or more, and per-hour estimates depend mechanically on the size of the cut, so its pooled figures don't map exactly onto the briefing's question.
- **The Halden 24-month subset** (+11.8%) comes from 14 of 23 organisations that responded. Non-responders may be disproportionately ones that reverted. Of the three that did revert, one was a marketing agency, so discretionary work with hard client deadlines can also fail. The coverage-bound/discretionary split doesn't capture this.

## Suggested Bottom line

> A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay reduces actual hours by about 11–14%. In discretionary work, the best available evidence (largely one randomised trial in public administration) shows output per actual hour rising by roughly 8–10%, enough to offset most but probably not all of the hours lost; a gain of this size persisted to two years, with some suggestion of decline. In the one setting tested, roughly half the gain was associated with fewer recurring meetings. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added. Costs per unit of output, effects beyond two years, and whether the gain requires the hours cut at all remain open.
